title: C# Program Structure, Syntax and Comments
learningObjectives: Identify statements, expressions, code blocks and the role of braces in C#.
Describe the conventional Main method entry point and modern top-level statements.
Apply basic syntax rules, including statement termination and case-sensitive identifiers.
Write single-line, multi-line and XML documentation comments appropriately.
Read a short C# program and predict its execution order and output.

understand.concept: A C# source file contains declarations and executable statements. A statement is an instruction; an expression produces a value; and braces group statements into a block. A console application can use top-level statements or an explicit Main method as its entry point. Comments explain source code to people and are ignored as executable instructions.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding program structure makes code easier to read, compile, debug and extend. It also helps beginners distinguish C# language rules from the project and runtime that execute a program.
understand.analogy: A C# program is like a written procedure: statements are individual instructions, braces group related steps, and comments are notes for the next person following the procedure.
understand.analogyLimit: Unlike an ordinary written procedure, C# has exact grammar rules. A missing semicolon or unmatched brace can prevent compilation even when the intended meaning seems obvious.

explain.narrative:
## Statements and expressions

A statement is a complete instruction, commonly ending with a semicolon. An expression such as `total + 5` produces a value and can be used inside a statement. C# identifiers are case-sensitive, so `total` and `Total` are different names.

## Blocks and braces

A block begins with `{` and ends with `}`. Classes, methods, namespaces and control-flow constructs commonly use blocks. Opening and closing braces must be paired, and indentation should make nesting visible.

## Entry-point styles

A traditional console application declares a `static Main` method inside a type. Modern C# also supports top-level statements, where executable statements appear directly in the source file. A source file must use one entry-point style consistently; do not place a second `Main` declaration inside another method.

## Comments

`//` starts a single-line comment. `/* ... */` marks a multi-line comment. `///` starts XML documentation comments, which tools can use to produce API documentation. Comments do not change program output and should explain intent, assumptions or public APIs rather than repeat every line.

## Version note

Top-level statements are supported from C# 9 onward. The CodeSaathi baseline is .NET 10 with C# 14. The examples below use syntax supported by that baseline.

examples.title: Top-level statements
examples.expectedOutput:
Program starts here
Each statement runs in order
examples.explanation: The compiler supplies the entry-point structure for this top-level program. Statements execute in source order.

examples.title: Traditional Main method
examples.explanation: The runtime starts this console program by invoking the static Main method. The braces delimit the class and method blocks.

examples.title: Statements inside a block
examples.explanation: The variable declaration and if statement are separate statements. The braces group the instruction that runs when the condition is true.

examples.title: Single-line and multi-line comments
examples.explanation: Both comment forms are ignored as executable instructions. The variable declaration and output statement still run.

examples.title: XML documentation comment
examples.explanation: Triple-slash comments provide XML documentation for declarations. They do not alter execution; the method returns a string that Main prints.

practise.guidedTask: Create a console program with a top-level entry point. Declare a variable, use an if block with braces, and add one useful single-line comment. Build and run it with .NET 10.
practise.independentTask: Rewrite the same small program using a traditional static Main method. Keep the output identical and explain which parts form the class block and method block.
hints: Pair every opening brace with a closing brace.
End ordinary statement instructions with semicolons.
Choose either top-level statements or an explicit Main entry point for each example.
Use comments to explain intent, not to restate obvious syntax.
practise.challenge: Add XML documentation comments to a public class and method, then inspect the generated documentation file in a separate project configured to produce XML documentation.
validationCriteria: The program compiles with the .NET 10 SDK and C# 14.
Exactly one entry-point style is used in each runnable example.
All braces and parentheses are balanced.
The observed output matches the expected output.
Comments do not change the program's runtime output.

questions.prompt: Which character commonly terminates a C# statement?
questions.explanation: Most ordinary C# statements end with a semicolon; block declarations use braces.

questions.prompt: What do braces { } primarily define in C#?
questions.explanation: Braces group statements into a block, such as a method or conditional body.

questions.prompt: Which entry-point style places executable statements directly in the source file?
questions.explanation: Top-level statements let a program begin with executable statements without explicitly writing Main.

questions.prompt: Which comment form is intended for XML API documentation?
questions.explanation: Triple-slash comments can be processed as XML documentation for declarations.
